foods.name: Milk
foods.preparation: 2% milk in most recipes; recipe 13 specifies pasteurized milk
foods.reason: Raw milk may contain harmful germs. Drink only pasteurized milk.
foods.safe_version: Choose pasteurized milk.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Quinoa
foods.preparation: cooked when a recipe lists cooked quinoa

foods.name: Tomatoes
foods.preparation: fresh or canned, as the recipe is written

foods.name: Lemon
foods.preparation: juice or whole, as the recipe is written

foods.name: Salmon
foods.preparation: frozen in the sheet-pan recipe; the superfood table also lists fresh or frozen
foods.reason: FDA lists salmon as a Best Choice. During pregnancy or breastfeeding, eat 2 to 3 servings a week from the Best Choices list. A serving is 4 ounces. Cook seafood to 145°F (63°C).
foods.safe_version: Choose salmon from the FDA Best Choices list and cook it to 145°F (63°C). Do not eat it raw.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish; cook temperature from FoodSafety.gov

foods.name: White beans
foods.preparation: cooked or canned, drained and rinsed when the recipe says so

foods.name: Greek yogurt
foods.reason: Only pasteurized milk products, including yogurt, are the kind this page says to consume.
foods.safe_version: Choose pasteurized yogurt.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Tilapia
foods.reason: FDA lists tilapia as a Best Choice. During pregnancy or breastfeeding, eat 2 to 3 servings a week from the Best Choices list. A serving is 4 ounces. Cook seafood to 145°F (63°C).
foods.safe_version: Cook tilapia to 145°F (63°C), until it is opaque.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish; cook temperature from FoodSafety.gov

foods.name: Sardines
foods.reason: FDA lists sardine as a Best Choice. During pregnancy or breastfeeding, eat 2 to 3 servings a week from the Best Choices list. A serving is 4 ounces.
foods.safe_version: Eat sardines from the Best Choices list, within 2 to 3 servings a week.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

foods.name: Eggs
foods.preparation: cooked until whites and yolks are fully set
foods.reason: Undercooked eggs may contain Salmonella. Cook eggs until the yolks and whites are firm.
foods.safe_version: Cook eggs until the yolks and whites are firm. Cook a dish that contains eggs to 160°F (71°C).
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Cheese
foods.reason: Avoid cheese made with unpasteurized milk, and avoid unheated queso fresco-type cheeses. Hard cheeses such as cheddar, Parmesan, and Swiss are listed when made with pasteurized milk. Cottage cheese, cream cheese, feta, and mozzarella are listed when made with pasteurized milk.
foods.safe_version: Check the label for pasteurized milk. Heat queso fresco-type cheese to 165°F or until steaming hot.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Canned tuna
foods.preparation: canned; the ingredient list says low-mercury varieties
foods.reason: FDA lists canned light tuna, including skipjack, as a Best Choice: 2 to 3 servings a week. Albacore or white tuna, canned or fresh, is a Good Choice: one serving that week and no other fish.
foods.safe_version: Choose canned light tuna. If the can says albacore or white tuna, eat only one 4-ounce serving that week and no other fish.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

foods.name: Canned salmon
foods.reason: FDA lists salmon as a Best Choice. During pregnancy or breastfeeding, eat 2 to 3 servings a week from the Best Choices list. A serving is 4 ounces.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

foods.name: Chicken thighs
foods.reason: Meat and poultry should be cooked thoroughly before eating, to the USDA-recommended safe minimum internal temperature.
foods.safe_version: Cook poultry thoroughly to the USDA-recommended minimum internal temperature.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Ground turkey
foods.reason: Meat and poultry should be cooked thoroughly before eating, to the USDA-recommended safe minimum internal temperature.
foods.safe_version: Cook ground turkey thoroughly to the USDA-recommended minimum internal temperature.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Cottage cheese
foods.reason: Cottage cheese is listed as a choice when it is made with pasteurized milk.
foods.safe_version: Choose cottage cheese made with pasteurized milk.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Iodized salt
foods.reason: The pantry list calls iodized salt an important source of iodine. That is a nutrient note, not a safety verdict.
foods.source_name: Superfood list.pdf: Affordable pantry staples

foods.name: Alcohol
foods.reason: There is no known safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy, no safe time to drink, and all types can be harmful, including wine, beer, and liquor.
foods.safe_version: Do not drink alcohol during pregnancy.
foods.source_name: CDC: About Alcohol Use During Pregnancy

foods.name: Caffeine
foods.reason: ACOG says moderate caffeine, less than 200 milligrams a day, has not been shown to cause miscarriage or preterm birth. That is about one 12-ounce cup of coffee. Caffeine is also in tea, chocolate, energy drinks, and soft drinks.
foods.safe_version: Keep total caffeine from all sources under 200 milligrams a day.
foods.source_name: ACOG: How much coffee can I drink while I'm pregnant?

foods.name: Raw fish
foods.reason: Raw seafood may contain parasites or germs, including Listeria. Cook seafood to 145°F (63°C). Avoid raw sushi, sashimi, raw oysters, raw clams, raw scallops, and ceviche.
foods.safe_version: Cook seafood to 145°F (63°C).
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Deli meat
foods.reason: Hot dogs, luncheon meats, cold cuts, and other deli-style meats may contain Listeria unless reheated.
foods.safe_version: Reheat until steaming hot or 165°F (74°C).
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Refrigerated smoked seafood
foods.reason: Refrigerated smoked seafood can contain Listeria. Do not eat it unless it is canned, shelf-stable, or cooked in a dish that reaches 165°F (74°C).
foods.safe_version: Choose canned or shelf-stable smoked seafood, or cook it to 165°F (74°C).
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Unpasteurized juice
foods.reason: Unpasteurized juice and cider, including fresh-squeezed juice, can contain E. coli and other germs.
foods.safe_version: Choose pasteurized juice, or boil unpasteurized juice or cider for at least 1 minute.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Raw milk
foods.reason: Raw milk may contain Campylobacter, E. coli, Listeria, Salmonella, or the bacteria that cause tuberculosis.
foods.safe_version: Choose pasteurized milk.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Queso fresco
foods.reason: Avoid unheated queso fresco-type cheeses, whether the milk was pasteurized or not, and avoid any cheese made with raw milk.
foods.safe_version: Heat queso fresco-type cheese to 165°F or until steaming hot.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Raw sprouts
foods.reason: Raw or undercooked sprouts may contain E. coli or Salmonella.
foods.safe_version: Cook sprouts thoroughly.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Premade deli salad
foods.reason: Do not buy or eat premade ham salad, chicken salad, or seafood salad from a deli. They may contain Listeria.
foods.safe_version: Skip premade deli meat and seafood salads.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Raw dough
foods.reason: Raw dough or batter can make you sick. Flour may contain E. coli, and raw eggs may contain Salmonella.
foods.safe_version: Bake or cook the batter thoroughly before eating.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Refrigerated pâté
foods.reason: Refrigerated pâté or meat spreads from a deli or the refrigerated section can contain Listeria.
foods.safe_version: Choose pâté in a can, jar, or sealed pouch that does not need refrigeration before opening, then refrigerate it after opening.
foods.source_name: FoodSafety.gov: People at Risk: Pregnant Women

foods.name: Shark
foods.reason: FDA lists shark under Choices to Avoid because of the highest mercury levels.
foods.safe_version: Choose a fish from the FDA Best Choices list instead.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

foods.name: Swordfish
foods.reason: FDA lists swordfish under Choices to Avoid because of the highest mercury levels.
foods.safe_version: Choose a fish from the FDA Best Choices list instead.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

foods.name: King mackerel
foods.reason: FDA lists king mackerel under Choices to Avoid because of the highest mercury levels.
foods.safe_version: Choose a fish from the FDA Best Choices list instead.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

foods.name: Bigeye tuna
foods.reason: FDA lists bigeye tuna under Choices to Avoid because of the highest mercury levels.
foods.safe_version: Choose canned light tuna or another Best Choice instead.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

foods.name: Marlin
foods.reason: FDA lists marlin under Choices to Avoid because of the highest mercury levels.
foods.safe_version: Choose a fish from the FDA Best Choices list instead.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

foods.name: Orange roughy
foods.reason: FDA lists orange roughy under Choices to Avoid because of the highest mercury levels.
foods.safe_version: Choose a fish from the FDA Best Choices list instead.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

foods.name: Albacore tuna
foods.reason: FDA lists albacore and white tuna as a Good Choice. Eat one serving that week and no other fish. A serving in pregnancy is 4 ounces.
foods.safe_version: Have only one 4-ounce serving of albacore or white tuna in a week, and no other fish that week. Canned light tuna is a Best Choice.
foods.source_name: FDA: Advice about Eating Fish

recipes.description: A quick pescatarian lunch combining inexpensive canned sardines, white beans, tomatoes, and whole-grain toast.
chef_tips: Canned sardines are shelf-stable and often less expensive than fresh fish.
FDA lists sardines among lower-mercury “Best Choices.”
Use gluten-free bread when necessary.
For a vegan version, leave off sardines and increase the beans to 2 cups.
recipes.superfood_spotlight: Sardines provide protein, omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin D, calcium when the edible bones are included, and other seafood nutrients.
benefits: FDA recommends 8–12 ounces per week of a variety of lower-mercury seafood during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Fish provides omega-3 fats, protein, iodine, choline, iron, vitamin D, and other nutrients relevant to pregnancy and lactation.
White beans add iron, folate, fiber, and choline.
Sardines with edible bones can also contribute calcium.
recipes.safety_note: FDA lists sardines among lower-mercury “Best Choices.”

steps.text: Combine white beans, tomatoes, lemon juice, and olive oil.

recipes.title: One-Pot Peanut Lentil & Sweet Potato Stew
recipes.description: A filling one-pot plant-based meal using inexpensive lentils, sweet potatoes, peanut butter, tomatoes, and spinach.
chef_tips: Red lentils cook quickly and require no soaking.
Frozen spinach keeps this inexpensive and convenient.
Use sunflower seed butter for a peanut-free version.
Serve alone or over rice if a higher-energy meal is needed.
The recipe is naturally vegan and gluten-free when all packaged ingredients are certified as needed.
recipes.superfood_spotlight: Lentils provide folate, iron, plant protein, fiber, and choline, while sweet potatoes provide beta-carotene.
benefits: Folate supports healthy fetal development and cell division.
Iron needs increase substantially during pregnancy.
Lentils are among the foods CDC identifies as sources of choline, whose needs increase during breastfeeding.
Sweet potatoes provide beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A.
Peanut butter adds energy, plant protein, and unsaturated fats.

ingredients.display: 4 cups low-sodium vegetable broth or water
Salt and black pepper to taste

steps.text: Add onion, garlic, lentils, sweet potato, tomatoes, ginger, paprika, and broth to a large pot.
Reduce heat and simmer for about 20 minutes or until the lentils and sweet potato are tender.
Add spinach and cook another 3–5 minutes.
